meta.date: ~600 BC (in vision, from the valley of Lemuel)

world_behind.title: Iron yokes were prophetic hardware
world_behind.text: The church that "yoketh them with a yoke of iron" (v. 5) borrows Jeremiah's stage prop: in Lehi's own decade, Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke to prophesy servitude, and when it was broken, the Lord promised yokes of iron instead (Jer. 28:13–14). For Nephi's hearers the image was recent public history, and it had ended badly.

cites.quote: yoketh them with a yoke of iron

spans.text: yoketh them with a yoke of iron

world_behind.title: John saw kindred scenes
world_behind.text: Gold, scarlet, fine linen, harlots, war on the saints: the vision's portrait of corrupt religion shares its wardrobe with the woman of Revelation 17 and its violence with the beast of Revelation 13. Two seers, centuries apart, given the same iconography for the same enemy.

world_behind.title: The nameless voyagers
world_behind.text: The record never names the "man among the Gentiles" (v. 12) or the multitudes that follow; readers since the book's first edition have seen the discovery voyages and colonial migrations here, and the text's own restraint is worth keeping: it describes offices, wrought upon, delivered, prospered.

world_behind.title: What the book's journey looked like
world_behind.text: Between "the mouth of a Jew" and the modern Gentile reader lie a thousand years of copying, translating, canon disputes, and institutional custody. The vision compresses that transmission history into one image, a book passing "through the hands of the great and abominable church" (v. 28), and grieves what fell out along the way.

cites.quote: through the hands of the great and abominable church

spans.text: through the hands of the great and abominable church

world_behind.title: Israel preserved the book
world_behind.text: "It proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew" (v. 23) is the vision's standing tribute: scripture's origin is Jewish speech, prophecy, and scribal labor. The record's later, sterner word to Gentiles who despise the Jews while living off their book (2 Ne. 29:4–5) begins in this verse's respect.

cites.quote: It proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew

spans.text: It proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew

world_behind.title: Many waters meant the ocean
world_behind.text: In Israel's poetry the sea is vastness and peril: they that go down to the sea in ships see the Lord's wonders in the deep (Ps. 107:23–24). The vision makes the ocean its stage twice over: first the divider protecting the remnant, then the highway the Spirit sends the Gentiles across.

words.text: The Spirit "came down and wrought upon the man" (v. 12): worked him, the way metal or dough is worked. The discovery of the new world is told entirely through that verb: history's famous crossings appear as the product of a Workman shaping willing material, and the workers themselves go unnamed.

cites.quote: came down and wrought upon the man

spans.text: came down and wrought upon the man

words.text: The covenant's own verb, handed to newcomers. What was promised this family on this land was conditional prosperity (1 Ne. 2:20); here the Gentiles "did prosper and obtain the land for their inheritance" (v. 15), on the same ground and under the same Spirit. The vision does not file them as trespassers on somebody else's promise. It puts them inside the promise, which is what makes the terms of chapter 14 theirs to answer.

cites.quote: did prosper and obtain the land for their inheritance

spans.text: did prosper and obtain the land for their inheritance

words.text: To pervert is to turn a thing aside from the course it was on. What the church does to the book is not called invention but diversion: parts taken away "that they might pervert the right ways of the Lord" (v. 27). Paul brought the same charge in the same words against a man working to keep a proconsul from believing (Acts 13:10). Both scenes fault the crooking of a road that was already straight.

cites.quote: that they might pervert the right ways of the Lord

spans.text: that they might pervert the right ways of the Lord

words.text: The theft's effect on ordinary readers: "an exceedingly great many do stumble" (v. 29). Nobody in the verse rejects the gospel; they trip over its gaps. The word carries the vision's tenderness toward the Gentile centuries: their blindness is described as an injury done to them, not a crime done by them.

cites.quote: an exceedingly great many do stumble

spans.text: an exceedingly great many do stumble

words.text: The Lord will not suffer the Gentiles to "utterly destroy the mixture of thy seed" (v. 30). Mixture is a blending word, used here and nowhere else in the record, and what it names is Nephi's line surviving inside his brothers' line. The preservation promised is of a mingled people, described as they would actually turn out to be.

cites.quote: utterly destroy the mixture of thy seed

spans.text: utterly destroy the mixture of thy seed

words.text: Hid up is not the same as lost. In this record it means put away on purpose, with the taking out already planned: the writings of Nephi's seed "shall be hid up, to come forth unto the Gentiles" (v. 35), the errand stated in the same breath as the burial. The phrase becomes the record's word for its own survival, and a thousand years later Ammaron will hide up the plates and then tell a ten-year-old where they are (Morm. 1:2–3).

cites.quote: shall be hid up, to come forth unto the Gentiles

spans.text: shall be hid up, to come forth unto the Gentiles

phrases.text: The vision's strongest loathing word is aimed with care: at an institution defined by its founder (the devil, v. 6), its conduct (slays, tortures, binds, yokes, v. 5), and its inventoried desires, "the gold, and the silver, and the silks, and the scarlets" (v. 8), "the praise of the world" (v. 9). No nation or denomination is named, and chapter 14 will supply the control: two churches only, sorted by whom they fight. The category is moral conduct, not a congregation, and any institution in any era can walk into or out of it.

cites.quote: the gold, and the silver, and the silks, and the scarlets

spans.text: the gold, and the silver, and the silks, and the scarlets

phrases.text: The ocean plays both of its parts in one panel: first the moat that "divided the Gentiles from the seed of my brethren" (v. 10), then the road the Spirit-driven ships cross. The same waters protect and deliver, depending on whose errand is on them; the vision's geography always answers to purpose.

cites.quote: divided the Gentiles from the seed of my brethren

spans.text: divided the Gentiles from the seed of my brethren

phrases.text: Three times in seven verses (v. 13, 16, 19) the colonizing Gentiles are described in the language of the exodus. The record files the future migrations with Israel's founding story (captivity, crossing, deliverance by God's power) and thereby claims those Gentile descendants as characters inside covenant history, with covenant accountability coming (ch. 14).

phrases.term: Proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew
phrases.text: The Bible's birth certificate in the vision's language: it came from a mouth, as spoken prophecy, Jewish speech, before it was ever a book. The phrase gives the record its settled posture toward the Bible: filial respect for the people whose mouth it came from.

The famous pair names two different losses. Plain things are clarity "unto the understanding of the children of men" (v. 29), scripture needing no guild to interpret. Precious things are the covenants and the weightier promises. Plainness in this record is a kindness, and its theft is the vision's real crime scene. The vision's restoration program (v. 34–35, 40) promises both back, and the record the reader is holding presents itself as that program's instrument.

cites.quote: unto the understanding of the children of men

spans.text: unto the understanding of the children of men

phrases.term: The book of the Lamb of God
phrases.text: By the panel's end the wounded book has a new name, ownership restored by title. Whatever was taken in transit, the vision never lets the Bible stop belonging to the Lamb, and the last records come forth to "establish the truth of the first" (v. 40).

cites.quote: establish the truth of the first

spans.text: establish the truth of the first

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: A man identified by what happened to him
verses.text: One of the most specific figures in the vision is given no name: "I beheld a man among the Gentiles, who was separated from the seed of my brethren by the many waters; and I beheld the Spirit of God, that it came down and wrought upon the man; and he went forth upon the many waters, even unto the seed of my brethren." Position, separation, influence and voyage are all supplied. The record never names him, here or anywhere else in the volume, and it names other individuals in this same chapter only by office.

verses.label: v. 20–24
verses.title: The provenance of another book, traced backwards
verses.text: The record follows a document to its source and states each stage. It is seen "carried forth among them," identified as proceeding "out of the mouth of a Jew," and then described at that point of origin: "when it proceeded forth from the mouth of a Jew it contained the fulness of the gospel of the Lord." Verse 25 adds the next stage, "these things go forth from the Jews in purity unto the Gentiles." A record makes a claim about the textual history of a different record, and it makes the claim in stages rather than all at once.

verses.label: v. 34–36
verses.title: A second book proposed as the repair
verses.text: The remedy is described as a document to be produced: "I will manifest myself unto thy seed, that they shall write many things which I shall minister unto them." Verse 36 states its contents in three terms, "in them shall be written my gospel, saith the Lamb, and my rock and my salvation." What is offered against the loss of plain and precious things is not a restoration of the damaged book but the writing of a new one, and the record says so before that book exists.

verses.label: v. 39–40
verses.title: The new records described by their function
verses.text: The record gives the purpose of the later writings in two clauses that do different jobs: they "shall establish the truth of the first, which are of the twelve apostles of the Lamb," and they "shall make known the plain and precious things which have been taken away from them." The first is corroboration and the second is supply. Verse 40 then names the specific content to be made known, "that the Lamb of God is the Son of the Eternal Father, and the Savior of the world."

chapter.title: A book prophesying about books
chapter.text: The vision's third panel is textual history: where the Bible came from, what happened to it, and what will be written to rescue its readers. The record's deepest self-understanding is on display. It exists because of what this chapter says was lost, and the reader is holding the instrument verse 35 commissions.

chapter.title: Corruption identified by appetite
chapter.text: The abominable church is diagnosed by desires and deeds, never by name, and the next chapter's two-church division confirms the category is functional. The record hands no sect a weapon here; it hands every institution, its own descendants' included, a mirror.

chapter.title: The Bible honored as a wounded parent
chapter.text: The account gives the book four stages in seven verses: "it proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew" at verse 23, it "contained the fulness of the gospel" at verse 24, it goes "from the Jews unto the Gentiles" in purity at verse 25, and plain and precious things are taken away at verse 26. Verse 40 then states the later record's own errand in relation to it, "these last records... shall establish the truth of the first, which are of the twelve apostles of the Lamb." The mission is stated as corroboration of the earlier book rather than replacement of it.

chapter.title: Gentile history inside covenant history
chapter.text: Discovery, colonization, and deliverance from the mother nations are told as an exodus, with God as the actor. The record refuses to leave the Gentiles outside the story, which also means they do not get to stay outside its accountability.

chapter.title: Mercy fences every wrath scene
chapter.text: The panel's darkest material is bracketed by neither-will-he-suffer clauses and closed by the Lamb's own mercy speech. Even the vision's judgment passages are structured as covenant restraint: wrath bounded, remnant kept, blindness scheduled to end.

chapter.title: The widening circles complete their sweep
chapter.text: Christ (ch. 11), the family's nations (ch. 12), and now all nations and their books. When chapter 15 shows the brothers refusing to ask about any of this, the reader will know the full size of what they declined.

applications.title: Run the desires audit
applications.text: The vision identifies corrupt religion by what it wants. Turn the instrument on your own practice of faith: list what you actually seek from your religion this month (comfort, standing, wealth, praise, or the saints' God) and let the list correct itself.

applications.title: Find the humbling inside the good stretch
applications.text: In a chapter full of crossings and empires, the hinge verse is the quiet one: the Gentiles who had gone out of captivity did humble themselves before the Lord, and the power of the Lord was with them. Prosperity follows the humbling here, and the seamanship gets no credit at all. Look back at a season of yours that went well and locate the humbling in it, because this record keeps putting that step exactly where you would expect to find the strategy.

applications.title: Read the Bible as a survivor
applications.text: Study it with the tenderness owed a wounded book: gratitude for the Jewish mouths and hands that carried it, patience with its hard places, and the restoration's witnesses open beside it to supply what transit cost.

applications.title: Keep things plain
applications.text: The vision's villains complicated scripture until ordinary people stumbled. Whatever you teach, whether class, family, or testimony, practice plainness as a form of kindness: one true thing, reachable words, no guild required.

applications.title: Let the books establish each other
applications.text: Build your study so the records corroborate: read the Bible and this record on the same doctrine in the same week, and write one sentence on what each establishes in the other. Testimony built on two witnesses holds in weather that topples one.

applications.title: Claim the verse 37 blessing on purpose
applications.text: The promise is for those who seek to bring forth Zion. Pick one act this month that is unambiguously Zion-work (a name to the temple, a neighbor served, peace published in your own house) and do it as a claim on the gift the verse attaches.

questions.text: Which of the church of desire's appetites (wealth, finery, indulgence, applause) currently has the easiest access to me?
Where in my own family's crossing story did the Spirit work on ordinary, nameless people, and have I told it that way?
Which plain thing have I made complicated, and who has stumbled on my version of it?
Do I extend to blinded people the vision's courtesy, treating them as injured, or do I grade them as if they had what was taken from them?
What did I actually do toward bringing forth Zion in the last month, in deeds a stranger could point to?
Where am I assuming a first place that the last-first inversion should make me hold more loosely?
